title: Dead while alive
hook: Kabir speaks of dying to ego while still living, and so being free

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's dog, and your line, led by the chain. Did you follow one small good tug? It's the end of a week with Kabir: a mother's tears, an elephant, a proud man, two shelves of books, a dog named Moti. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

Some people go quiet when the subject of dying comes up. Change the topic. Knock on wood. Kabir does something stranger. He talks about death as if it were good news. Not someday, at the end, but now, today, while the heart is still beating. For two days he's been lowering himself: the worst of all, the Lord's dog. Today we find out where that road goes. It goes somewhere that sounds, at first, like a contradiction. Today: dead while alive.
screen: `SOME PEOPLE CHANGE THE TOPIC.` → `KABIR CALLS IT GOOD NEWS.` → `WHERE THE LOW ROAD GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's one of Kabir's saloks. The dying that the world fears, he says, brings joy to my mind. Because it's through dying that perfect bliss is found. Now, Kabir isn't longing for a funeral. Sikh readers hear in this a different death: the death of the ego, the I that grabs and compares and insists on its own way. Haumai, Sikhs call it, the sense of I, me, mine. It's the thing that kept a proud man sure his birth made him higher. It's the thing that points at everyone else's faults. This week's hymns have been slowly loosening it. When it finally lets go, something is left that's lighter and freer, and still breathing. That's today's word. Jeevan mukat. Jeevan is life. Mukat is freedom, release. Free while living. Sikh teaching doesn't place freedom only after death, in some far-off place. It can be tasted here, at the kitchen sink, at the loom, in traffic. The person who's free while living still works, still eats, still loves their family. Kabir kept singing. What has died is the grip. Try it with your hands. You're holding a hot pan by the handle, knuckles white, scared to drop it. Now set it down. Your hand is still your hand. It's just not clenched anymore. That's the kind of dying Kabir is talking about: the clench goes, the hand stays. So the line we carry out of this week is not about the end of life. It's about the middle of it. Free while living.
screen: `THE DYING THE WORLD FEARS.` · `HAUMAI: I, ME, MINE.` · `JEEVAN MUKAT: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `THE CLENCH GOES, THE HAND STAYS.` · then, large: `FREE WHILE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one ego-want go. Settle, and breathe. Find one small thing your I is gripping right now. Wanting the last word. Wanting credit. Wanting someone to notice you were right. Don't fight it. Just name it, and on each out-breath, loosen your hold by a little, like setting down a hot pan. See what's left when the clench goes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Jeevan mukat. Free while living: released from the grip of ego here and now, not only after death.
Your line: free while living. Look back over this week with Kabir, and let one grip from it go today, a grudge, a need to win, a fear of what people think. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of jeevan mukat as freedom from ego while living an ordinary householder's life, and Kabir's saloks on dying to the self are sung and explained in kirtan and katha.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: liberated while living, free from ego here and now.

notes: Salok paraphrased; confirm Ang 1365 and the rendering ('jis marne te jag darai, mere man anand; marne hi te paaiai pooran parmanand').
'Jeevan is life. Mukat is freedom' gives word meanings, not a derivation; confirm. Gurmukhi ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ and 'JEE-van MUK-at': confirm.
Haumai glossed as 'I, me, mine'; confirm.
'Sikh teaching doesn't place freedom only after death' and the householder framing: general teaching, not cited to a specific line; confirm.
Week end (day 756): look-back placed in review and carry.
